etymology.text: From the root ر ب ع; Wiktionary: spring (season); spring grain; spring vegetation, pasture. Plurals أَرْبِعَة, أَرْبِعَاء, رِبَاع.

funFacts: One of its plurals, أَرْبِعَاء, is spelled like Wednesday (Wiktionary).
Two months of the Islamic calendar are named after it: ربيع الأول and ربيع الآخر.
pitfalls: Masculine: الرَّبِيعُ جَمِيلٌ.
It shares the letters ر ب ع with أَرْبَعَة (four) and رُبْع (a quarter).
subtleties: The seasons are usually definite: فِي الرَّبِيعِ, الرَّبِيعُ قَادِمٌ.

etymology.text: Wiktionary: perhaps a euphemism for قَيْظ, the word for “summer” in other West Semitic languages, from the root ص ف و “to be clear”. Plurals أَصْيَاف, صُيُوف.

funFacts: مَصِيف is a summer resort, and صَيْفِيّ “summer” as an adjective: مَلَابِسُ صَيْفِيَّةٌ (summer clothes).
pitfalls: صَيْف (summer, with ص) and ضَيْف (guest, with ض) sound alike to beginners.
subtleties: “In summer” is فِي الصَّيْفِ or simply صَيْفًا.

pitfalls: خَرِيف (autumn) and خَرُوف (sheep) differ in one vowel letter.
subtleties: In Sudan الْخَرِيف is the rainy season in the middle of the year.

funFacts: Hebrew סְתָו (stav) is the same old word — and means autumn; in the Levant شِتِي is also “rain”.
pitfalls: The final hamza: شِتَاءٌ, شِتَاءً (no extra alif).
subtleties: In Levantine speech عَم تِشْتِي means “it is raining”: winter is the rainy season.

pitfalls: The plural أَسَابِيعُ is diptote: بَعْدَ أَسَابِيعَ (after some weeks).
subtleties: “Next week” and “last week” are accusatives of time: الْأُسْبُوعَ الْقَادِمَ, الْأُسْبُوعَ الْمَاضِيَ.

pitfalls: Two plurals: أَشْهُر, mostly after 3–10 (ثَلَاثَةُ أَشْهُرٍ), and شُهُور (general).

etymology.text: Wiktionary: inherited from Proto-Semitic *šanat-; cognate to Hebrew שָׁנָה and Ugaritic šnt.

funFacts: Hebrew שָׁנָה (shana) is the same word: רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה and رَأْسُ السَّنَةِ both mean “the head of the year”.
pitfalls: Feminine: سَنَةٌ جَدِيدَةٌ. Plural سَنَوَات (also سِنُونَ / سِنِينَ, formal).
After 11–99 the singular accusative: عِشْرُونَ سَنَةً.
subtleties: سَنَة and عَام are interchangeable in most uses; عَام is masculine.

subtleties: Formal style prefers عَام: الْعَامُ الدِّرَاسِيُّ, عَامُ ٢٠٢٦.

funFacts: Telling the time uses it with an ordinal: السَّاعَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ = three o’clock (lit. the third hour).

pitfalls: كَمِ السَّاعَةُ؟ — كَمْ takes a helping kasra before al-.

subtleties: One word for hour, clock and watch — the context decides.

The usual birthday wish is كُلَّ سَنَةٍ وَأَنْتَ بِخَيْرٍ.
pitfalls: My birthday = عِيدُ مِيلَادِي: the owner ending goes on the second word, the case on the first (عِيدِ مِيلَادِي after a preposition).
subtleties: A construct of two words: plural أَعْيَادُ مِيلَادٍ; “the birthday” is said with an owner (عِيدُ مِيلَادِهِ), since عِيدُ الْمِيلَادِ suggests Christmas.

profile.feeling: No school, no work: rest and travel.

examples.tr: Have a nice holiday!
Friday is a day off.
We travel during the holidays.

synonyms.nuance: holiday, leave from work — the usual word in Egypt and the Gulf; also “permission, licence”
a feast: a religious or national holiday

etymology.text: From the root ع ط ل, “to be idle, to be out of work”; Wiktionary: vacation, holiday (plurals عُطْلَات, عُطَل).

funFacts: Same root as مُعَطَّل, “out of order”: on a holiday work stands still.
pitfalls: Two plurals: عُطْلَات and عُطَل.
subtleties: عُطْلَة is time off; a feast with its rites is عِيد (عِيدُ الْفِطْرِ).

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: The time before something happens.

examples.tr: I drink coffee before breakfast.
Wash your hands before eating.
I arrived an hour ago.

profile.synonymsNone: The only “before” in time; “in front of” (place) is أَمَامَ.

etymology.text: From the root ق ب ل (front; to face, to receive); Wiktionary: before, prior to; ago.

funFacts: The same root gives قِبْلَة, the direction faced in prayer, and مُسْتَقْبَل, the future.
pitfalls: قَبْلَ is time; in front of a place is أَمَامَ (lesson 12).
The noun after it is genitive: قَبْلَ الظُّهْرِ; pronouns are endings: قَبْلِي, قَبْلَكَ.
subtleties: قَبْلَ + a span of time = ago: قَبْلَ يَوْمَيْنِ (two days ago).

meaningForms.what: with -u, after a negation: yet (لَمْ يَصِلْ بَعْدُ)

profile.feeling: What comes next.

senses.def: in (a time from now): بَعْدَ أُسْبُوعٍ (in a week)
yet — بَعْدُ (with -u) after a negation: لَمْ يَصِلْ بَعْدُ (he has not arrived yet)

examples.tr: We drink tea after lunch.
I’m travelling in a week.
After you!

examples.text: لَمْ يَصِلِ الْقِطَارُ بَعْدُ، سَيَصِلُ بَعْدَ عَشْرِ دَقَائِقَ.
examples.tr: The train hasn’t arrived yet; it will arrive in ten minutes.

synonyms.nuance: right after, immediately following

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the preposition بَعْدَ, “after”; from the root ب ع د (to be far).

funFacts: Same root as بَعِيد (far, lesson 12) — a handy memory link: after = further on.
pitfalls: بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ is a fixed word for the afternoon (lesson 14).
بَعْدُ with -u, alone, means “yet”: لَمْ يَصِلْ بَعْدُ (he hasn’t arrived yet).
subtleties: بَعْدَ + a span of time = in (from now): بَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ (in an hour).

root.none: a basic preposition (a short particle)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: A limit in time: up to that point.

senses.def: so that, in order to (a conjunction)

examples.tr: I work until the evening.
Wait until tomorrow.
Even the children know that.

synonyms.nuance: to, until — especially in مِنْ … إِلَى … (from … to …)
up to, until

etymology.text: Wiktionary: grammarians link it to the root ح ت ت (to end something), an irregular derivation; some classical dialects have عَتَّى, closer to Ugaritic ʿd, Hebrew עַד and Aramaic ʿad.

funFacts: Wiktionary connects it with Hebrew עַד (ad, until).
pitfalls: The noun after it is genitive: حَتَّى الْمَسَاءِ; in modern style it takes no pronoun endings.
subtleties: It can also mean “even”: حَتَّى أَنَا (even I).

root.none: a basic preposition (a short particle)

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

profile.feeling: From a point in the past up to now.

senses.def: for (a period up to now); ago (with a past verb)

examples.tr: I’ve been waiting since the morning.
I’ve been living here for a year.
How long have you been studying Arabic?

synonyms.nuance: since — a shorter form (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the preposition مُنْذُ, marking the time at which something started or the length of time up to now; alternative form مُذْ.

funFacts: Like German seit and Greek εδώ και, it goes with the present tense: أَعِيشُ هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَةٍ = Ich wohne seit einem Jahr hier — not a perfect as in English.
pitfalls: For something still going on use the present tense: أَعْمَلُ هُنَا مُنْذُ سَنَتَيْنِ.
The noun after it is genitive: مُنْذُ الصَّبَاحِ.
subtleties: With a past verb it means “ago”: وَصَلَ مُنْذُ سَاعَةٍ (he arrived an hour ago).

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

contrasts.value: during, within a period; مِنْ خِلَالِ “through”

profile.feeling: A span of time and what fills it.

senses.def: مِنْ خِلَالِ … — through, by way of

examples.tr: During the holidays we travel.
I’ll arrive within an hour.
During the week I work a lot.

synonyms.nuance: during — while something else happens
throughout, all through

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of the plural of خَلَل (“gap”), i.e. “between the gaps of”.

funFacts: Literally “in the gaps of” — time seen as a space you move through.
pitfalls: مِنْ خِلَالِ means “through, by means of”, not “during”.
subtleties: خِلَالَ looks at the whole span (within a week); أَثْنَاءَ at what happens at the same time (during the meal).

profile.feeling: At the same time as something else.

examples.tr: I don’t talk while eating.
The child slept during the trip.
I read a book during the journey.

synonyms.nuance: during, within — the whole span
during, in the course of

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the adverbial accusative of أَثْنَاء, the plural of ثِنْي (“a fold; a single repetition; time”).

funFacts: Same root as اِثْنَانِ (two): ثِنْي is a fold, a doubling.
pitfalls: The hamza is on the line: أَثْنَاءَ; with pronouns أَثْنَاءَهُ, أَثْنَائِي.
subtleties: Very common with a verbal noun: أَثْنَاءَ الْعَمَلِ (while working), أَثْنَاءَ الْأَكْلِ (while eating).

absent.use: The hour is said with السَّاعَةُ (the hour) + an ordinal number in the feminine: السَّاعَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ = five o’clock (lit. “the fifth hour”); one o’clock is السَّاعَةُ الْوَاحِدَةُ. “At five” = فِي السَّاعَةِ الْخَامِسَةِ (or عِنْدَ …). In everyday speech the cardinal number is common: السَّاعَة خَمْسَة. The ordinals come later in the course; see the table in “Time: before, after …” (lesson 15).
